_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla, typed out on the slip. Each lesson has two: "start" comes on as the lesson opens, and "check" is a short quiz once the lesson's check is done. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies" (none means a plain "Roger. Over."). A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. First rain of the season reached the coast Saturday. Aberdeen says a low a day lined up out to sea now, through April. This week, why all winter and none all summer, and why some of it floods.

replies.say: Something to do with the high?
replies.back: Half of it. The high, and the wind upstairs.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Questions. Why does the coast stay dry in July?

replies.say: The high sits off the coast and the lows go by up north.
replies.back: Right. They come back south with the fall.
No. The lows just aren’t coming that way. The high’s off the coast and the storm track’s up by Alaska.
Plenty of water. Nothing to lift it. The lows pass far to the north.

turns.them: Same storm, same water, two Februarys. One the snow line’s at two thousand feet, the other at seven thousand. Which floods the rivers?

replies.back: Right. Rain clear up the mountains, and running off the same day.
Other way. With a low snow line most of it sits up there as snow until June.
Same water, but the high snow line sends it all down the river at once.

turns.them: Last one. Wind northwest behind the front. Downpour at Everett, sun in Seattle. Why?

replies.say: The wind splits round the Olympics and meets itself.

replies.back: Not quite. The two streams round the Olympics meet over the Sound and the air goes up.
Front’s long gone. It’s the wind closing up again behind the Olympics.
